problem: Existing visual navigation foundation models (GNM, ViNT, NoMaD) use low-capacity CNN encoders without pretrained weights that model observation and goal as a whole, and are pretrained on limited, non-diverse data, so they generalize poorly to OOD environments.
motivation: Image-goal navigation requires fine-grained correspondence between the current view and the goal image, and pretrained navigation models need broad data to transfer zero-shot and fine-tune with little labeled data. Game videos are abundant but unlabeled, and global decision-making supervision is missing from pure waypoint prediction.
key_idea: Use an early-fusion, self-supervised-pretrained (MAE) ViT over patch tokens of both observation and goal, train with auxiliary global tasks (relative pose, distance, global path), and augment pretraining with IDM-labeled game videos.
insight: Early fusion of low-level patch features, MAE-initialized ViT and global auxiliary losses each give consistent gains; e.g. zero-shot avg SR on Highrise is 0.487 (non-fuse) vs 0.693 (early fuse), and ViT-raw 0.380 vs DINOv2 0.600 vs MAE 0.693. MAE outperforms DINOv2, hypothesized because it preserves fine-grained detail rather than high-level semantics. Auxiliary tasks matter mostly in zero-shot (waypoint-only 0.613 vs all 0.693 on Highrise), and game data lowers validation loss (0.189 to 0.164).
method: Early-fusion ViT: observation and goal images are patchified, tagged with learnable obs/goal embeddings, and jointly fed with a [CLS] token into one ViT-Base encoder so attention operates across low-level patches of both images.
Pretrained encoder init: ViT initialized from self-supervised MAE (or DINOv2); MAE found best.
Waypoint action head: MLP on [CLS] predicts next 10 waypoints in [dx, dy, cos dψ, sin dψ] with position-yaw L2 loss.
Auxiliary tasks: relative pose of goal, navigation distance, and global path (10 equally time-spaced waypoints to goal) predicted from the [CLS] embedding.

Game video pipeline: 220k gameplay videos (~2,000 games) cut into 10 s clips; two-step Qwen2-VL-7B prompt filtering (precision 52%→85%, recall 75%→68%); an Inverse Dynamics Model trained on open nav datasets labels actions.
Pretraining data: GoStanford, RECON, CoryHall, BDD100k, SCAND, TartanDrive, SACSoN plus labeled game video, with outlier filtering and normalization; then fine-tune per environment.

setting.backbone: ViT-Base (MAE-pretrained init), ~100M params, early-fusion, fine-tuned end-to-end
setting.training_data: Open nav datasets (GoStanford, RECON, CoryHall, BDD100k, SCAND, TartanDrive, SACSoN) plus IDM-labeled game videos (from 220k videos, ~2,000 games); fine-tuning on 2,100 human episodes in the ShooterGame environments and 113 real robot episodes
setting.observation: monocular RGB current image (90° FOV) + goal image
setting.action_space: predicted waypoints (10 steps of [dx, dy, cos dψ, sin dψ])
setting.simulator: ShooterGame (Unreal Engine 4): Highrise and Sanctuary maps

numbers.eval_set_note: 50 random start-goal tasks per difficulty level (Easy)

numbers.extra: fine-tuned on Sanctuary episodes; Easy 1.00/0.96, Medium 0.84/0.75

numbers_note: Custom benchmarks (not canonical). Table 1 gives per-difficulty results; only Hard, Easy, or Medium rows listed partially (unlisted values are given in the extra field or in Table 1). Data-efficiency results are only in figures.
results: PIG-Nav beats GNM, ViNT and NoMaD in both zero-shot and fine-tuned settings across Highrise, Sanctuary and a real robot, e.g. zero-shot Sanctuary Easy SR 0.84 vs best baseline 0.41 (ViNT), and real robot ZS SR 0.50 vs 0.13 (ViNT). Claims average +22.6% (zero-shot) and +37.5% (fine-tuning) SR, and about 8x less fine-tuning data needed.
limitations: Evaluation is on custom game environments and a small real-robot test (8 tasks) with no standard benchmarks, and the gains from game data are shown only via validation loss, not navigation SR.
Smaller pretraining data than GNM/ViNT/NoMaD; no memory or topological map, so long-horizon exploration in unseen environments is limited.
